```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Yan 2017 sets a dose of **cyadox**, a quinoxaline-1,4-dioxide antibacterial
developed for veterinary use, against *Clostridium perfringens*, the cause of
necrotic enteritis in pigs. Free cyadox was sampled from the ileum lumen of
pigs through implanted ultrafiltration probes after a single 30 mg/kg oral dose,
and each ileum-fluid sample was then challenged ex vivo with the pathogenic
strain CPFK122995. The 24 h change in bacterial count was related to the
PK/PD index AUC0-24h/MIC with an inhibitory sigmoid Emax model (equation (1),
fitted in WinNonlin 5.2).

| Model file | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `Yan_2017_cyadox_pkpd_index` | Ex vivo inhibitory sigmoid Emax model, 24 h change in log10 CFU/mL vs AUC0-24h/MIC, ileum fluid | Equation (1), Table 4 |

The pharmacokinetics in the paper are non-compartmental only (Table 2), so no
PK model file is packaged; see *Assumptions and deviations*.

* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03970-9>

```{r model}
mod <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Yan_2017_cyadox_pkpd_index"))
```

# Population

Six healthy castrated crossbred pigs (Duroc x Large White x Landrace,
15-20 kg) had an ultrafiltration probe implanted in the ileum about 30 cm
proximal to the ileocaecal orifice and were dosed orally with cyadox 30 mg/kg
48 h after surgery. Ileum fluid and plasma were sampled from 0 to 24 h. The
free ileum-fluid concentrations peaked at 23.66 ug/mL at 1.96 h and were
roughly 500-fold higher than the plasma concentrations (Table 2).

*C. perfringens* CPFK122995 is a pathogenic pig isolate whose cyadox MIC,
2 ug/mL in both Brucella broth and ileum fluid, equals the MIC50 of 60 clinical
isolates from Guangdong (Figure 2). In the ex vivo time-kill assay about
10^6 CFU/mL of CPFK122995 were incubated anaerobically in each ileum-fluid
sample and counted up to 24 h (limit of detection 10 CFU/mL). The model takes
no animal covariates, so no virtual cohort is needed; every simulation below is
a deterministic typical-value solve.

# Source trace

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sigmoid Emax equation | `E = Emax - (Emax - E0)*C^N/(C^N + EC50^N)` | Equation (1) |
| Paper's Emax (drug-free change) -> `e0` | 2.71 log10 CFU/mL | Table 4 |
| Paper's E0 (maximal kill) -> `emax` | -4.61 log10 CFU/mL | Table 4 |
| Emax - E0 (consistency row) | 7.32 log10 CFU/mL | Table 4 |
| EC50 | 30.07 h | Table 4 |
| N (Hill coefficient) | 4.62 | Table 4 |
| Targets for E = 0 / -3 / -4 | 26.72 / 39.54 / 50.69 h | Table 4 |
| MIC of CPFK122995 (`mic`) | 2 ug/mL | Results, MIC/MBC/PAE section |
| Ex vivo inoculum (`log10_cfu0`) | 10^6 CFU/mL | Methods, time-kill study |
| Ex vivo exposure `AUC_CYADOX` | 24 h x sample concentration | Equation (1) definition of C |
| Ileum-fluid NCA | Cmax 23.66 ug/mL, AUC0-inf 112.35 h*ug/mL | Table 2 |
| MIC distribution of 60 isolates | 0.5-8 ug/mL | Figure 2 |
| Dose equation | `Dose = CL x (AUC/MIC)BP x MIC / (F x fu)` | Equation (2) |
| Predicted daily doses | 13.2 / 19.70 / 25.46 (50%), 29.3 / 42.56 / 54.50 (90%) mg/kg | Table 5 |

# Table 4 target indices

Table 4 prints the AUC0-24h/MIC that gives no net change (E = 0), a 3-log10
kill (E = -3) and a 4-log10 kill (E = -4). These are an answer key for the
equation form and for which Table 4 row is the drug-free effect. The packaged
model is solved over a fine grid of exposures and the 24 h change is
interpolated at each target.

```{r targets}
mic <- 2
cfu0 <- 1e6
grid_aucmic <- exp(seq(log(1), log(1000), length.out = 800))
ex_events <- function(aucmic) {
  data.frame(
    id = seq_along(aucmic), time = 24, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "bact",
    AUC_CYADOX = aucmic * mic
  )
}
sim_grid <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ex_events(grid_aucmic), returnType = "data.frame")
# The 24 h change is read from the bacterial state itself; the `log_cfu`
# output adds a 1 CFU/mL floor that biases it by up to 0.02 log10 near
# the maximal kill.
dE <- log10(sim_grid$bact) - log10(cfu0)

targets <- data.frame(
  E = c(0, -3, -4),
  published = c(26.72, 39.54, 50.69)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = approx(dE, grid_aucmic, xout = E)$y,
    pct_diff = 100 * (model - published) / published
  )
targets |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = round(model, 2), pct_diff = round(pct_diff, 2)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Target E (log10 CFU/mL)" = E,
    "Published AUC0-24h/MIC (h)" = published,
    "Model AUC0-24h/MIC (h)" = model,
    "Difference (%)" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 4 target indices, published versus solved from the packaged model.")
```

```{r targets-check}
stopifnot(
  # All three printed targets reproduce to better than 0.5%.
  all(abs(targets$pct_diff) < 0.5)
)
```

All three targets reproduce to within 0.4%. Reading the paper's Emax and E0 the
conventional way round (Emax as the maximal kill) would make the curve rise from
-4.61 to +2.71 with exposure, so the bacterial kill would weaken as the drug
concentration increased and the elimination target would fall at the lowest
index rather than the highest.

# Ex vivo ODE versus the closed-form equation

The model integrates the bacterial density so that its log10 changes by exactly
the equation (1) value over 24 h. Both sides use the same parameters, so the
difference is pure numerical error and is held to a tight bound.

```{r ode-check}
closed_form <- function(x) {
  2.71 - (2.71 - (-4.61)) * x^4.62 / (x^4.62 + 30.07^4.62)
}
stopifnot(
  all(abs(dE - closed_form(grid_aucmic)) < 1e-3),
  # Drug-free control and saturation.
  abs(closed_form(0) - 2.71) < 1e-12,
  abs(dE[length(dE)] - (-4.61)) < 1e-2
)
```

# Effect curve (replicates Figure 6)

```{r fig6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 6 of Yan 2017: 24 h change in C. perfringens CPFK122995 count versus ex vivo AUC0-24h/MIC. Dashed lines mark the bacteriostatic (0), bactericidal (-3) and elimination (-4) levels; points mark the Table 4 targets."}
data.frame(aucmic = grid_aucmic, change = dE) |>
  dplyr::filter(aucmic <= 300) |>
  ggplot(aes(aucmic, change)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "navy") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, -3, -4), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = targets, aes(published, E), colour = "firebrick", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "AUC0-24h/MIC (h)", y = "Change in log10 CFU/mL over 24 h") +
  theme_bw()
```

The curve starts at +2.71 for drug-free ileum fluid and plateaus at -4.61, as
in Figure 6. The largest index plotted in Figure 6, about 285 h, is the peak
ileum-fluid sample: 23.66 ug/mL x 24 h / 2 ug/mL = 283.9 h.

# Exposure after the 30 mg/kg oral dose

Table 3 integrates the in vivo ileum-fluid AUC0-24h (106.40 h*ug/mL in
Table 2) with the MIC to give an AUC0-24h/MIC of 66.39 h. The model places that
exposure on the plateau, beyond the elimination target, which is the paper's
basis for concluding that 30 mg/kg is efficacious against strains with an MIC of
2 ug/mL.

```{r in-vivo-index}
sim_iv <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod,
  data.frame(id = 1, time = 24, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "bact", AUC_CYADOX = 66.39 * mic),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)
change_iv <- log10(sim_iv$bact) - log10(cfu0)
round(change_iv, 2)
stopifnot(change_iv < -4)
```

# Predicted daily doses (Table 5)

Equation (2), `Dose = CL x (AUC/MIC)BP x MIC / (F x fu)` with F = fu = 1, was
combined in a Monte Carlo simulation with the apparent clearance of the six
pigs and the MIC distribution of the 60 isolates. The paper prints the mean
apparent clearance (0.27 L/kg/h, which equals 30 mg/kg / 112.35 h*ug/mL) but not
its spread, so the clearance is taken here as log-normal with the coefficient of
variation of AUC0-inf in Table 2 (14.07 / 112.35 = 12.5%). The MIC distribution
is read from Figure 2 as 2, 11, 25, 19 and 3 isolates at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and
8 ug/mL; those counts reproduce the plotted percentages (3.3, 18.3, 41.7, 31.7
and 5.0%), the MIC50 of 2 and the MIC90 of 4 ug/mL. The dose that attains a
target in a given fraction of the population is then a quantile of the
required-dose distribution, computed exactly rather than by sampling.

```{r doses}
mic_tab <- data.frame(mic = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), n = c(2, 11, 25, 19, 3))
stopifnot(sum(mic_tab$n) == 60)
auc_m <- 112.35
auc_sd <- 14.07
sdlog <- sqrt(log(1 + (auc_sd / auc_m)^2))
mu_cl <- log(30) - (log(auc_m) - sdlog^2 / 2)

tar_dose <- function(target, p) {
  cdf <- function(d) {
    sum(mic_tab$n / 60 * pnorm((log(d / (target * mic_tab$mic)) - mu_cl) / sdlog)) - p
  }
  uniroot(cdf, c(0.1, 1000), tol = 1e-10)$root
}
doses <- expand.grid(endpoint = c("Bacteriostatic (E = 0)", "Bactericidal (E = -3)", "Elimination (E = -4)"), tar = c(0.5, 0.9)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    target = rep(targets$published, 2),
    published = c(13.2, 19.70, 25.46, 29.3, 42.56, 54.50),
    model = mapply(tar_dose, target, tar),
    ratio = published / model
  )
doses |>
  dplyr::mutate(tar = paste0(100 * tar, "%"), model = round(model, 2), ratio = round(ratio, 3)) |>
  dplyr::select(endpoint, tar, published, model, ratio) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Endpoint" = endpoint, "Target attainment" = tar,
    "Table 5 dose (mg/kg/day)" = published, "Recomputed dose (mg/kg/day)" = model,
    "Published / recomputed" = ratio
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table 5 daily doses versus doses recomputed from equation (2), Table 2 and Figure 2.")
```

```{r doses-check}
stopifnot(
  # The six published doses sit a near-constant factor below the recomputed
  # ones, so the targets and the MIC distribution are consistent with Table 5
  # and the gap lies in the clearance input (see Assumptions and deviations).
  diff(range(doses$ratio)) < 0.05,
  all(doses$ratio > 0.83 & doses$ratio < 0.93)
)
```

Every Table 5 dose is 0.87-0.90 times the recomputed value. Because the factor
is the same for all three endpoints and both attainment levels, it does not come
from the PK/PD targets, which enter the dose proportionally, nor from the MIC
distribution, which would distort the 50% and 90% columns differently. It
corresponds to a central apparent clearance of about 0.24 L/kg/h instead of the
0.27 L/kg/h reported in the Abstract; the individual clearances the paper used
are not printed, so this is noted and not adjusted.

# PKNCA

There is no PKNCA section. The packaged model has no pharmacokinetic state: the
paper reports only a non-compartmental analysis of the ileum-fluid and plasma
concentrations (Table 2) and no structural PK model, so there is no simulated
concentration-time profile to analyse. The exposure that drives the model is
supplied as the `AUC_CYADOX` covariate.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Emax and E0 naming.** The Methods prose describes Emax as the maximal drug
  effect and E0 as the effect in drug-free ileum fluid. Equation (1), however,
  returns Emax at zero exposure, Table 4 gives Emax = +2.71 (net growth) and
  E0 = -4.61 (net kill), Figure 6 starts near +2.7 and plateaus near -4.6, and
  the three Table 4 targets reproduce only under that reading. The model
  therefore maps the paper's Emax onto the canonical `e0` and the paper's E0
  onto the canonical `emax`. No value is changed.
* **No PK model.** Yan 2017 analysed the pharmacokinetics non-compartmentally
  only. A one-compartment model with first-order absorption cannot be
  reconstructed from Table 2: with CL/F = 30 / 112.35 = 0.267 L/kg/h, an
  elimination rate of ln(2)/5.86 h and an absorption rate solved from
  Tmax = 1.96 h, it predicts a peak of 10.5 ug/mL against the observed
  23.66 ug/mL. The exposure is therefore supplied as a covariate, as in the
  paper's own PK/PD integration.
* **Ex vivo inoculum.** The ex vivo time-kill curves are stated to follow the
  in vitro procedure, whose starting inoculum is 10^6 CFU/mL; that value is used
  for `log10_cfu0`. The predicted 24 h change does not depend on it.
* **Variability.** Table 4 reports mean +/- SD of the estimates; no
  between-animal variance or residual error was estimated, so the model has no
  random effects and `addSd` is fixed at 0.
* **Clearance spread in the dose check.** The paper does not print the
  individual or the SD of the apparent clearance used in its Monte Carlo
  simulation; the dose check above assumes a log-normal clearance with the
  coefficient of variation of AUC0-inf. The MIC counts are read from Figure 2.
* **Conclusions versus Table 5.** The Conclusions give 17.90 mg/kg as the
  bactericidal dose for 50% target attainment; Table 5 and the Results give
  19.70 mg/kg. The Table 5 value is used above.
* **Errata.** No erratum or correction to Yan 2017 was found (Europe PMC,
  checked 2026-11-25).
